desc:
A directed graph has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1; each edges[i] = [from, to, w] is a one-way edge of weight w (negative values allowed). A cycle is a closed walk v0 → v1 → … → v0; a self-loop is a cycle of one edge. The mean of a cycle is its total weight divided by its number of edges.

Find the cycle with the smallest mean (nodes of the walk may repeat, but repeating nodes never gives a smaller mean than the best simple cycle). Return that minimum mean as the reduced fraction [p, q] with q > 0 and gcd(|p|, q) = 1; the value 0 is written [0, 1]. If the graph has no cycle, return the empty array [].

Example: n = 3, edges = [[0,1,2],[1,2,-1],[2,0,5]]. The only cycle has weight 6 and 3 edges, mean 2, answer [2, 1]. For n = 4, edges = [[0,1,3],[1,0,-4],[2,3,1]] the cycle 0 → 1 → 0 has mean -1/2, so the answer is [-1, 2]. A graph with only [[0,1,1],[1,2,1]] has no cycle: [].
constraints: edges[i] = [from, to, w] with 0 ≤ from, to < n and -1,000 ≤ w ≤ 1,000
Each ordered pair (from, to) appears at most once; from may equal to
hints: Compare cycles by mean, not by total weight. Guessing the mean and checking with a negative-cycle test (subtract the guess from every weight) works with binary search on rationals but is awkward to make exact.
Karp's algorithm: let D[k][v] be the cheapest walk with exactly k edges that ends at v and may start anywhere (so D[0][v] = 0). Any walk of n edges contains a cycle.

The minimum mean is the minimum over nodes v with finite D[n][v] of the maximum over k in 0..n-1 of (D[n][v] - D[k][v]) / (n - k). Compare fractions by cross-multiplication, then reduce by the gcd. If every D[n][v] is infinite, there is no cycle.
editorial: Karp's theorem gives the minimum cycle mean in O(n · E) time with the same table you would use for Bellman-Ford with exact edge counts. Fill D[0][v] = 0 for all v (every node may start a walk) and D[k][v] = min over edges (u,v,w) of D[k-1][u] + w. The value D[n][v] is finite only if a walk with n edges ends at v, and any such walk repeats a node and therefore contains a cycle; if no D[n][v] is finite the graph is acyclic.

Karp's formula: mu = min over v of max over k of (D[n][v] - D[k][v]) / (n - k), taken over nodes v with finite D[n][v] (then all D[k][v], k ≤ n, are finite as well, since a walk of n edges has suffixes of every shorter length). Intuitively, for a node v on the best cycle, the best n-edge walk to v reaches the cycle early and then circles around it, so the maximum over k exposes the cycle's mean. Keep the fractions as integer pairs and compare with cross-multiplication to stay exact; all weights are integers so the result is a rational with denominator at most n. Complexity: O(n · E) time to fill the table, O(n2) for the final scan and space.
